of the Crestbone Crossing project included the construction of a new Round Top Road from I-10 to FM 518 and the construction of a new junction at the Arroyo Grande Segment and Saddle Ridge Road (W86).

The construction was the largest rail project in TxDOT history at 3.9 million tons. Known as the Crestbone Crossing project, it extended the existing rail line from its existing line through the Town of Inks Lake to a new segment of track in the Arroyo Grande and through a new junction into the Texas North Country.

The project opened three new bridges, including one of the largest bridges ever built for rail in the United States, which increased total rail crossing capacity in the area by almost 2,000 vehicles. Under the five year contract, TxDOT planned to handle at least 85,000 vehicle miles daily, 2,400 rail vehicles per day, and 120 rail yards per day of widened rail and bridges.

A record 825 trailers, 47 rail cars, 153 track elements, 717 technical vehicles, 74 platforms and 20 spurs were used to complete the project. Work began in early August, 2009.

The advent of terraced fields in the 2nd and the middle ages reduced the growth of trees in major cities. Meanwhile, stone masonry construction developed in the 4th and spread into lower regions. This conformed to the well-known saying "whatever can be built, has been built". The statue was expanded with many additional elements to reflect these changes. Within the Roman inscriptions the statue of San Lorenzo depicts a horse-riding saint, God, and an obscure man beside a man standing on a cliff and a young boy playing a conch shell. The saddle with the young boy on it is the representation of the neck, which hinged at the shoulder to gain greater mobility. 2002 in Ypres, Belgium. Although originally intended to help in the search for lost British soldiers, the area of ruins now known as Menin Gate was chosen because the site was recognisable from reconnaissance photographs taken when the Allies captured Ypres. It is the final resting place of several hundred British soldiers killed in the Battle of Ypres in 1917.

Photo © The British War Graves Commission

Menin Gate was a very low, square and very flat brick wall with a small weather overhang and paved roadway running along the west side of the base of the wall. The gate was built and reinforced in the first months after the war to provide temporary shelter for wounded and missing soldiers, and that remained its function up until its closure on 7 September 1960.

After being used as a temporary soldier's hut, the wall was covered with sheets of corrugated iron to form a trench with room for a gun, and walls were set back from the edge of the concrete and piece-iron construction to create a covered walkway. The alluvial lining was then poured to create the space between the two concrete blocks, and over the top of this was partitioned the space below for the status of the dead to be recorded.
